newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong to U.S. air cargo market booming.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong to U.S. air cargo market booming.

text.p: The air cargo market from Hong Kong to the U.S. is booming with backlogs building up as supply of freighter space fails to keep pace with early peak season demand, a Reuters survey shows.

A 30 per cent hike in cargo rates is also predicted within the industry as some airlines prepare for their second rate rise within a month. China Airlines led the way raising its ex Hong Kong trans-Pacific rate by around HK$2.30 on July 1 with some other carriers following mid month.

China Airlines is raising rates again on August 1 and rival airlines are expected to follow suit to take advantage of what has quickly become a sellers market. Airlines hope peak market conditions will stretch all the way to November or even Christmas to cap what has so far been a busier year than normal.
Trans-Pacific average rates which are now around HK$18-19 are expected to rise to between HK$22-23 within the next month, especially when existing contracts expire, industry sources said.
Forwarding agents generally said because margins have been low they will not be able to absorb the forthcoming rate rise and expect to pass most of it onto their customers.
"Traffic is tremendous with a backlog of more than three or four days for some airlines," reported one well known forwarder.
China Airlines, a major ex Hong Kong cargo carrier to its Taipei hub, mirrored the general airline comment by saying "business is booming."
As well as demand for scheduled services, the Taiwanese flag carrier is also enjoying unexpectedly high demand for direct charter flights to the U.S. from Hong Kong's Kai Tak airport.

"Three charter flights a week, two to New York and one to Chicago, are planned from the middle of August from Hong Kong to cope with demand," said a spokesman. China Airlines currently offers daily dedicated Boeing 747 freighter flights between the Taiwanese capital and the U.S. west coast in addition to New York, Chicago and Miami, a Hong Kong spokesman said.

Hong Kong's de facto flag carrier, Cathay Pacific Airways Limited, which traditionally takes the lead in setting rates which other airlines usually follow, said it will also raise rates from August 1. Cathay said the selling rate from August 1 will be between HK$22-23 per kilo, a rise of HK$2 on July rates.
"Things are on fire right now with strong demand ex Hong Kong," said one Cathay source.

Cathay is enjoying full freighter flights to New York and Chicago but demand for space back to Hong Kong is disappointing as the U.S. holiday season takes its effect. Ex-U.S. rates are reported to be remaining stable. Cathay does not expect ex-U.S. demand to pick up until the end of August.
"That market (ex-U.S.) is ticking over rather than doing anything spectacular for us at the moment," the Cathay source said.

"1997 has been an exceptional year compared to last year where demand has been quite consistent. The U.S. market usually fluctuates a lot and the peak usually starts later but this year, even in the slack season in April and May demand was there," said another Cathay spokesman.
Cathay expects the U.S. market peak season to now stretch until mid December.

Trans-Pacific rivals, Northwest Airlines, also reported high tonnages of freight in the market with the peak season definitely arrived. Northwest plans to raise rates on August first but the amount has not been decided yet, said Alexander Wong, Northwest's cargo sales and marketing manager in Hong Kong.
"Space is very tight and demand is high," Wong said
Sources said Northwest has some of the lowest trans-Pacific rates currently on offer.

One factor thought to be responsible for unexpectedly high demand can be traced back to a handful of trans-Pacific cargo flights which were cancelled over the handover holiday period reducing ex Hong Kong capacity by more than 1,000 tonnes. Carriers have been struggling to catch up since.
"It was supposed to be a holiday but we didn't expect so much cargo to build up," said one airline representative.

"The peak season has started already with the trans-Pacific market very strong," reported Anthony Lau, the chairman of the 261 member Hong Kong Association of Freight Forwarding Agents Ltd who is also chairman and chief executive of BALtrans Holdings Ltd.

"Everyone is reporting a busy time which is a good sign. The market to the U.S. is very strong because of a strong U.S. economy demanding large amounts of products from this region especially toys and garments," he added.
Mattel is reported to be one major exporter of toys to the U.S. with McDonald's hamburger chain also reported to shifting large amounts of children's give-away gifts to its U.S. heartland.
Compared to the trans-Pacific market, demand for space to Japan only is reported to be weaker in comparison. Much ex Hong Kong cargo goes through airline hubs in Japan.

Nippon Cargo Airlines (NCA) reported 90 per cent of cargo on its four weekly Boeing 747-200 freighter flights from Hong Kong to Tokyo Narita and Osaka Kansai is destined for the American market. NCA has 13 freighter flights a week from Japan to U.S. east and west coast destinations, New York and San Francisco. NCA is to increase its west coast schedule by one more frequency per week from September, said its sales and reservations manager in Hong Kong, Michael Wu.

The cargo subsidiary of All Nippon Airways is also about to expand its fleet to eight B747-200 freighters to operate intra-Asian destinations such as Singapore and Bangkok but not Hong Kong in the short term because of slot restrictions at both Kai Tak and Japan's main cargo destination, Tokyo Narita.

Cathay said its important outbound cargo market to Japan was strong, especially to Narita which is Hong Kong's second busiest export destination. But compared to previous years, growth has not been as robust.
The market to Japan's other main ex Hong Kong destination, Osaka Kansai, has also been weaker, probably as a result of extra capacity on the route.
The Japanese market remains Cathay's highest yield for cargo, despite the extra capacity, a spokesman said.

For instance, Hong Kong's all cargo airline, AHK Air Hong Kong has withdrawn from the Chicago market and added an extra frequency to Osaka creating another 100 tonnes of capacity. Cathay has also added a wide bodied passenger flight to Osaka adding belly cargo capacity.

The Hong Kong-Japan sector also has extra capacity an the shape of Air India which is offering discounted belly cargo rates to try and build market share, its Hong Kong cargo manager, Kevin Fung, said.

The Indian flag carrier now operates five flights a week between Bombay and Hong Kong, four of them continuing onto either the Seoul or Osaka in Japan. Since the beginning of July, Air India has extended two of its three Airbus A310 flights a week between Bombay and Hong Kong onto Seoul and also operates a twice weekly service between Bombay and Osaka via Hong Kong. The Wednesday service utilises a Boeing 747-200 passenger aircraft, the Sunday flight a B747-300 Combi aircraft with around 50 tonnes capacity.
The carrier admits competition is tough from airlines such as Cathay Pacific and Japan Airlines which offer high quality service and more frequencies.

Asiana Airlines reported high loads ex Hong Kong to Seoul. A Hong Kong spokesman reported backlogs in Seoul for its trans-Pacific destinations to Los Angeles, San Francisco, New York, Chicago and Seattle.

"The slow season is almost finished and the peak season is already here which will last until the end of the year. Rates have also been rising," the Asiana spokesman said but declined to detail by how much. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
